template.name: Opening: A Town of Peculiar Habits

assignments.text:
Oh! it was an awful time; coming down like a thunder-bolt on the still sunny
day when the lilacs were all in bloom.”
assignments.summary: Miss Matty reflects on the tragedy as a sudden, devastating thunderbolt striking on an otherwise beautiful and peaceful spring day.
assignments.best_quote: Oh! it was an awful time; coming down like a thunder-bolt on the still sunny day when the lilacs were all in bloom.

assignments.text:
“Oh, gentility!” thought I, “can you endure this last
shock?” For Miss Barker had ordered (nay, I doubt not, prepared, although she
did say, “Why, Peggy, what have you brought us?” and looked pleasantly
surprised at the unexpected pleasure) all sorts of good things for
supper—scalloped oysters, potted lobsters, jelly, a dish called “little
Cupids” (which was in great favour with the Cranford ladies, although too
expensive to be given, except on solemn and state occasions—macaroons
sopped in brandy, I should have called it, if I had not known its more refined
and classical name).
assignments.summary: A second tray arrives with supper: scalloped oysters, potted lobsters, jelly, and 'little Cupids' (macaroons sopped in brandy), sumptuous fare that tests genteel propriety.
assignments.best_quote: Oh, gentility! thought I, can you endure this last shock?

assignments.text:
There were one or two
robberies—real  bonâ fide  robberies; men had up before the
magistrates and committed for trial—and that seemed to make us all afraid
of being robbed; and for a long time, at Miss Matty’s, I know, we used to make
a regular expedition all round the kitchens and cellars every night, Miss Matty
leading the way, armed with the poker, I following with the hearth-brush, and
Martha carrying the shovel and fire-irons with which to sound the alarm; and by
the accidental hitting together of them she often frightened us so much that we
bolted ourselves up, all three together, in the back-kitchen, or store-room, or
wherever we happened to be, till, when our affright was over, we recollected
ourselves and set out afresh with double valiance.
assignments.summary: Every night, Miss Matty, Mary, and Martha conduct an armed expedition through the house to check for robbers, often frightening themselves so badly they lock themselves in the back kitchen.
assignments.best_quote: Miss Matty leading the way, armed with the poker, I following with the hearth-brush, and Martha carrying the shovel and fire-irons with which to sound the alarm

template.name: The Genteel Trap: Miss Matty's Slow Unravelling

assignments.text:
“Elegant economy!” How naturally one falls back into the phraseology of
Cranford! There, economy was always “elegant,” and money-spending always
“vulgar and ostentatious”; a sort of sour-grapeism which made us very peaceful
and satisfied.
assignments.summary: The narrator reflects on how Cranford inverses values: economy becomes elegant and spending becomes vulgar, a sour-grape philosophy that creates social peace.
assignments.best_quote: 'Elegant economy!' How naturally one falls back into the phraseology of Cranford!

assignments.text:
But when she was gone Miss Pole began
a long congratulation to Miss Matty that so far they had escaped marriage,
which she noticed always made people credulous to the last degree; indeed, she
thought it argued great natural credulity in a woman if she could not keep
herself from being married; and in what Lady Glenmire had said about Mr
Hoggins’s robbery we had a specimen of what people came to if they gave way to
such a weakness; evidently Lady Glenmire would swallow anything if she could
believe the poor vamped-up story about a neck of mutton and a pussy with which
he had tried to impose on Miss Pole, only she had always been on her guard
against believing too much of what men said.
assignments.summary: After Lady Glenmire leaves, Miss Pole congratulates Miss Matty and Mary on their unmarried state, arguing that marriage makes women credulous and that spinsters like herself are superior in judgment.
assignments.best_quote: she thought it argued great natural credulity in a woman if she could not keep herself from being married

assignments.text:
We were thankful, as Miss Pole desired us to be, that we had never been
married; but I think, of the two, we were even more thankful that the robbers
had left Cranford; at least I judge so from a speech of Miss Matty’s that
evening, as we sat over the fire, in which she evidently looked upon a husband
as a great protector against thieves, burglars, and ghosts; and said that she
did not think that she should dare to be always warning young people against
matrimony, as Miss Pole did continually; to be sure, marriage was a risk, as
she saw, now she had had some experience; but she remembered the time when she
had looked forward to being married as much as any one.
assignments.summary: Mary and Miss Matty silently disagree with Miss Pole; Miss Matty privately reflects that she views marriage as protection against danger and recalls once hoping to marry.
assignments.best_quote: she did not think that she should dare to be always warning young people against matrimony, as Miss Pole did continually; to be sure, marriage was a risk, as she saw, now she had had some experience; but she remembered the time when she had looked forward to being married as much as any one

assignments.text:
“Not to any particular person, my dear,” said she, hastily checking herself up,
as if she were afraid of having admitted too much; “only the old story, you
know, of ladies always saying, ‘ When  I marry,’ and gentlemen, ‘ If 
I marry.’” It was a joke spoken in rather a sad tone, and I doubt if either of
us smiled; but I could not see Miss Matty’s face by the flickering fire-light.
In a little while she continued—
assignments.summary: Miss Matty hastily corrects herself, joking about the old convention that ladies expect to marry while gentlemen merely consider it, though her tone suggests sadness.
assignments.best_quote: Not to any particular person, my dear, said she, hastily checking herself up, as if she were afraid of having admitted too much; only the old story, you know, of ladies always saying, 'When I marry,' and gentlemen, 'If I marry.'

assignments.text: “But, after all, I have not told you the truth.
assignments.summary: Miss Matty signals that she has not been fully honest and is about to reveal something significant about her past.
assignments.best_quote: But, after all, I have not told you the truth.

assignments.text:
God ordains it all, and I am
very happy, my dear. No one has such kind friends as I,” continued she, taking
my hand and holding it in hers.
assignments.summary: Miss Matty concludes that God has ordained her fate and she is content, finding happiness in her friendships despite her lost love.
assignments.best_quote: God ordains it all, and I am very happy, my dear. No one has such kind friends as I

assignments.text:
“And my father, my dear, dear father! I will not complain now, if God will give
me strength to be patient. But, oh, Jessie! tell my father how I longed and
yearned to see him at last, and to ask his forgiveness. He can never know now
how I loved him—oh! if I might but tell him, before I die! What a life of
sorrow his has been, and I have done so little to cheer him!”
assignments.summary: Miss Brown grieves that she never told her father she loved him or asked his forgiveness, and that she did little to alleviate his sorrowful life.
assignments.best_quote: And my father, my dear, dear father! I will not complain now, if God will give me strength to be patient. But, oh, Jessie! tell my father how I longed and yearned to see him at last, and to ask his forgiveness. He can never know now how I loved him—oh! if I might but tell him, before I die! What a life of sorrow his has been, and I have done so little to cheer him!

assignments.text:
Instead of tying up preserves in the
store-room, however, we went to talk in the dining-room; and there Miss Jenkyns
told me what Major Gordon had told her; how he had served in the same regiment
with Captain Brown, and had become acquainted with Miss Jessie, then a
sweet-looking, blooming girl of eighteen; how the acquaintance had grown into
love on his part, though it had been some years before he had spoken; how, on
becoming possessed, through the will of an uncle, of a good estate in Scotland,
he had offered and been refused, though with so much agitation and evident
distress that he was sure she was not indifferent to him; and how he had
discovered that the obstacle was the fell disease which was, even then, too
surely threatening her sister.
assignments.summary: Miss Jenkyns explains that Major Gordon served with Captain Brown and fell in love with Miss Jessie when she was young; he proposed when he inherited a Scottish estate but was refused because of her sister's illness.
assignments.best_quote: how he had served in the same regiment with Captain Brown, and had become acquainted with Miss Jessie, then a sweet-looking, blooming girl of eighteen; how the acquaintance had grown into love on his part, though it had been some years before he had spoken; how, on becoming possessed, through the will of an uncle, of a good estate in Scotland, he had offered and been refused, though with so much agitation and evident distress that he was sure she was not indifferent to him; and how he had discovered that the obstacle was the fell disease which was, even then, too surely threatening her sister.

assignments.text:
She had mentioned that the surgeons foretold
intense suffering; and there was no one but herself to nurse her poor Mary, or
cheer and comfort her father during the time of illness. They had had long
discussions; and on her refusal to pledge herself to him as his wife when all
should be over, he had grown angry, and broken off entirely, and gone abroad,
believing that she was a cold-hearted person whom he would do well to forget.
assignments.summary: Major Gordon learned that Miss Jessie refused him because she must care for her sister during illness and comfort her father; he grew angry and left England, believing her cold-hearted.
assignments.best_quote: she had mentioned that the surgeons foretold intense suffering; and there was no one but herself to nurse her poor Mary, or cheer and comfort her father during the time of illness. They had had long discussions; and on her refusal to pledge herself to him as his wife when all should be over, he had grown angry, and broken off entirely, and gone abroad, believing that she was a cold-hearted person whom he would do well to forget.

assignments.text:
He had been travelling in the East, and was on his return home when, at Rome,
he saw the account of Captain Brown’s death in  Galignani .
assignments.summary: Major Gordon was traveling in the East and saw Captain Brown's death reported in an Italian newspaper, prompting his return to England.

assignments.text:
A light came into Miss Jessie’s face. “Would it comfort you, dearest, to think
that he does know?—would it comfort you, love, to know that his cares,
his sorrows”—Her voice quivered, but she steadied it into
calmness—“Mary! he has gone before you to the place where the weary are
at rest. He knows now how you loved him.”
assignments.summary: Miss Jessie gently tells her sister that their father is already dead and in heaven, where he now knows how much she loved him.
assignments.best_quote: Would it comfort you, dearest, to think that he does know?—would it comfort you, love, to know that his cares, his sorrows—Her voice quivered, but she steadied it into calmness—Mary! he has gone before you to the place where the weary are at rest. He knows now how you loved him.

assignments.text:
“No, madam. I must draw a line somewhere. Mrs Jamieson would not, I think, like
to meet Mrs Fitz-Adam. I have the greatest respect for Mrs Fitz-Adam—but
I cannot think her fit society for such ladies as Mrs Jamieson and Miss Matilda
Jenkyns.”
assignments.summary: Miss Betty Barker declines to invite Mrs Fitz-Adam, despite respecting her, as she is unsuitable company for ladies of higher rank.
assignments.best_quote: I cannot think her fit society for such ladies as Mrs Jamieson and Miss Matilda Jenkyns.

assignments.text:
Many a farmer’s wife or daughter turned away huffed from
Miss Barkers’ select millinery, and went rather to the universal shop, where
the profits of brown soap and moist sugar enabled the proprietor to go straight
to (Paris, he said, until he found his customers too patriotic and John Bullish
to wear what the Mounseers wore) London, where, as he often told his customers,
Queen Adelaide had appeared, only the very week before, in a cap exactly like
the one he showed them, trimmed with yellow and blue ribbons, and had been
complimented by King William on the becoming nature of her head-dress.
assignments.summary: Mary describes how rival shopkeepers attracted farmers' wives by falsely claiming royal endorsements, contrasting with Miss Barkers' commitment to truth and exclusivity.
assignments.best_quote: Queen Adelaide had appeared, only the very week before, in a cap exactly like the one he showed them, trimmed with yellow and blue ribbons, and had been complimented by King William on the becoming nature of her head-dress.

assignments.text:
I have loved her ever since, though
perhaps I’d no right to do it; but if you can think of any way in which I might
be allowed to give a little more without any one knowing it, I should be so
much obliged to you, my dear. And my brother would be delighted to doctor her
for nothing—medicines, leeches, and all.
assignments.summary: Mrs Fitz-Adam admits she has loved Miss Matty since that day and offers her brother's medical services to help her.
assignments.best_quote: I have loved her ever since, though perhaps I'd no right to do it

assignments.text:
But the present customer stood opposite to her, without asking for anything,
only looking fixedly at her as he drummed upon the table with his fingers, just
for all the world as Miss Jenkyns used to do. Miss Matty was on the point of
asking him what he wanted (as she told me afterwards), when he turned sharp to
me: “Is your name Mary Smith?”
assignments.summary: The mysterious customer suddenly turns to Mary and asks her name, causing her to realize his identity.
assignments.best_quote: Is your name Mary Smith?

assignments.text:
This remedy, perhaps, was recommended by some
one of the number whose advice she asked; but the proposal, if ever it was
made, was knocked on the head by Captain Brown’s decided “Get her a flannel
waistcoat and flannel drawers, ma’am, if you wish to keep her alive. But my
advice is, kill the poor creature at once.”
assignments.summary: Captain Brown offers decisive practical advice: either clothe the cow in flannel or put it out of its misery.
assignments.best_quote: Get her a flannel waistcoat and flannel drawers, ma'am, if you wish to keep her alive. But my advice is, kill the poor creature at once.

assignments.text:
It was full of love, and sorrow, and pride in his new profession, and a sore
sense of his disgrace in the eyes of the people at Cranford; but ending with a
passionate entreaty that she would come and see him before he left the Mersey:
“Mother; we may go into battle. I hope we shall, and lick those French: but I
must see you again before that time.”
assignments.summary: Peter's letter to his mother expresses love, sorrow for his disgrace, and pride in his naval profession, ending with a passionate plea to see her before possible battle.
assignments.best_quote: 'Mother; we may go into battle. I hope we shall, and lick those French: but I must see you again before that time.'

assignments.summary: The father suddenly declares that the shawl must be the mother's burial cloth, giving Peter the comfort of knowing his gift honored her.
assignments.best_quote: 'She shall be buried in it,' he said; 'Peter shall have that comfort; and she would have liked it.'

assignments.text:
On the whole, we were rather
glad to hear this, for she had made a pleasant impression upon us; and it was
also very comfortable to find, from things which dropped out in the course of
conversation, that, in addition to many other genteel qualities, she was far
removed from the “vulgarity of wealth.”
assignments.summary: The narrator notes that the Cranford ladies are pleased to discover Lady Glenmire is not vulgar or ostentatious despite her title.
assignments.best_quote: it was also very comfortable to find, from things which dropped out in the course of conversation, that, in addition to many other genteel qualities, she was far removed from the "vulgarity of wealth."

assignments.text:
One honest-looking man, however, made his way up to the counter
at which we stood, and boldly asked to look at a shawl or two. The other
country folk confined themselves to the grocery side; but our neighbour was
evidently too full of some kind intention towards mistress, wife or daughter,
to be shy; and it soon became a question with me, whether he or Miss Matty
would keep their shopmen the longest time.
assignments.summary: An honest-looking farmer approaches their counter boldly to view shawls, contrasting with the shyness of other country folk.
assignments.best_quote: One honest-looking man, however, made his way up to the counter at which we stood, and boldly asked to look at a shawl or two

template.name: Laughter as Survival: Humor and Social Endurance

assignments.text:
It is said—I won’t vouch for the fact—that Captain Brown was heard
to say,  sotto voce , “D—n Dr Johnson!” If he did, he was penitent
afterwards, as he showed by going to stand near Miss Jenkyns’ arm-chair, and
endeavouring to beguile her into conversation on some more pleasing subject.
But she was inexorable. The next day she made the remark I have mentioned about
Miss Jessie’s dimples.
assignments.summary: The Captain is rumoured to have cursed Dr Johnson sotto voce; he attempts reconciliation but Miss Jenkyns remains unforgiving and later criticises Miss Jessie's dimples.
assignments.best_quote: he was heard to say, sotto voce, "D—n Dr Johnson!"

assignments.text:
She accordingly mixed a
saucerful for him, and put it down for him to lap; and then she told us how
intelligent and sensible the dear little fellow was; he knew cream quite well,
and constantly refused tea with only milk in it: so the milk was left for us;
but we silently thought we were quite as intelligent and sensible as Carlo, and
felt as if insult were added to injury when we were called upon to admire the
gratitude evinced by his wagging his tail for the cream which should have been
ours.
assignments.summary: Mrs Jamieson praises Carlo's refined taste in rejecting milk, while the ladies silently resent being considered less discriminating than the dog.
assignments.best_quote: She accordingly mixed a saucerful for him, and put it down for him to lap; and then she told us how intelligent and sensible the dear little fellow was; he knew cream quite well, and constantly refused tea with only milk in it: so the milk was left for us; but we silently thought we were quite as intelligent and sensible as Carlo, and felt as if insult were added to injury when we were called upon to admire the gratitude evinced by his wagging his tail for the cream which should have been ours.

assignments.text:
The signora told me, one day, a good deal about their lives up to this period. It began by my asking her whether Miss Pole’s story of the twin-brothers were
true; it sounded so wonderful a likeness, that I should have had my doubts, if
Miss Pole had not been unmarried.
assignments.summary: Mary asks the Signora if Miss Pole's story about the twin brothers is true; notes she would doubt it but trusts Miss Pole's unmarried status ensures accuracy.

assignments.text:
If all parties were agreeable, Martha and Jem were to be
married with as little delay as possible, and they were to live on in Miss
Matty’s present abode; the sum which the Cranford ladies had agreed to
contribute annually being sufficient to meet the greater part of the rent, and
leaving Martha free to appropriate what Miss Matty should pay for her lodgings
to any little extra comforts required. About the sale, my father was dubious at
first.
assignments.summary: Mary and her father plan that Martha and Jem will marry and remain in Miss Matty's house while taking her as a lodger, with the ladies' contributions paying most rent.

assignments.text:
This was the first letter, ticketed in a frail, delicate hand, “From
my dearest John.” Shortly afterwards they were married, I suppose, from the
intermission in their correspondence.
assignments.summary: The bride's letter responding to the gift is labeled 'From my dearest John' in her delicate hand; their correspondence then ceases, implying they married.
assignments.best_quote: From my dearest John

assignments.text:
Miss Pole had once asked her for the receipt, but she had met with a
very decided rebuff; that lady told her that she could not part with it to any
one during her life, and that after her death it was bequeathed, as her
executors would find, to Miss Matty.
assignments.summary: Miss Pole once asked Mrs Forrester for the bread-jelly receipt but was refused; Mrs Forrester has instead bequeathed it to Miss Matty in her will.
assignments.best_quote: she could not part with it to any one during her life, and that after her death it was bequeathed, as her executors would find, to Miss Matty

assignments.text:
“But I don’t pretend to understand business; I only
know that if it is going to fail, and if honest people are to lose their money
because they have taken our notes—I can’t explain myself,” said she,
suddenly becoming aware that she had got into a long sentence with four people
for audience; “only I would rather exchange my gold for the note, if you
please,” turning to the farmer, “and then you can take your wife the shawl.
assignments.summary: Miss Matty explains that she cannot allow honest people to lose money because of her bank's notes, even if she cannot articulate her reasoning clearly.
assignments.best_quote: if it is going to fail, and if honest people are to lose their money because they have taken our notes—I can't explain myself, only I would rather exchange my gold for the note, if you please
